title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Operational Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning practices, reliability initiatives, incident review requirements, operational tooling, and the canonical runbook templates used by on-call engineers. It consolidates existing runbook guidance and formalizes escalation and remediation workflows to ensure consistent, auditable responses and driven reliability improvements.

Audience
- SRE and production engineering teams
- Service owners and product managers
- Incident commanders and on-call engineers

Goals
- Ensure measurable, defensible SLOs across customer-visible services.
- Provide clear error budget governance to guide rollouts and mitigations.
- Maintain capacity buffers to absorb traffic spikes and component failures.
- Standardize incident review and reliability initiative workflows to close postmortem action items.
- Provide practical runbooks and operational tooling references for rapid, safe remediation.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Principles
- SLOs must be customer-centric: availability, end-to-end latency, and correctness for user-facing APIs.
- Each service has a single primary SLO and up to two secondary SLOs.
- SLOs should be expressed as percentage targets over a rolling 30-day window unless otherwise justified.

Required SLOs (recommended defaults)
- Redwood API (text generation endpoints): Availability 99.9% over 30 days; 95th percentile latency < 250 ms for short-form requests (<=512 tokens).
- Inference Serving (Dedicated pools): Availability 99.95% over 30 days; 95th percentile tail latency < 350 ms for typical model workloads.
- Console (UI/API): Availability 99.5% over 30 days; median response time < 150 ms.

Error budget governance
- Error budget = 1 - SLO target over the evaluation window.
- Burn rate monitoring: define burn-rate thresholds (green/yellow/red):
  1. Green: burn <= 1x expected (normal operation).
  2. Yellow: burn > 1x and <= 4x — owner notified, mitigate non-breaking releases, increase monitoring cadence.
  3. Red: burn > 4x — freeze non-critical rollouts; convene emergency reliability review within 4 hours.

Rollout policy tied to error budget
- If error budget is in Yellow for 6+ hours: pause all canary/gradual rollouts for the affected service and roll back last deploy if symptomatic.
- If error budget is in Red: initiate rollback to last known good, unlock incident playbook, and notify platform ops and product leadership.

SLO ownership and measurement
- Each service must declare an SLO owner (on the service README). SLO metrics must be emitted to the central metrics tier (Prometheus/Tempo/ClickHouse pipeline) with documented metric names and tags.
- Measurement method must be defensible: client-observed metrics for availability, trace-derived latency metrics for p95/p99.

SLO example configuration (text format)
- service_name: redwood-api-generation
- primary_slo: availability
- target: 99.9
- window_days: 30
- metric: http_requests_success_ratio{service="redwood-api-generation"}

2) Capacity Planning

Principles
- Capacity plans must be forward-looking (12 months) and updated quarterly.
- Plans include traffic forecasts (QPS, token/sec), headroom targets, hardware mix (GPU types, vCPU/memory for control plane), and recovery runways.
- Maintain at least two recovery strategies: fast-scale (autoscaling or burst pools) and longer-term provisioning (capacity purchases / reserved pools).

Headroom and thresholds
- Standard headroom targets by criticality:
  - Tier 1 (customer-facing inference APIs): 30% steady-state headroom at 95th percentile traffic.
  - Tier 2 (internal tooling / console): 20% headroom.
  - Tier 3 (non-critical batch jobs): 10% headroom.

Forecasting data inputs
- Historical telemetry (90/95/99th percentiles), on-call incident logs, marketing/launch calendars, customer committed capacity, planned model onboarding (model memory and perf profiles), and expected retention/usage changes after product launches.

Capacity runbook checklist (quarterly)
1. Validate traffic forecasts against actuals and update the 12-month forecast.
2. Confirm GPU pool utilization: target average utilization 60-75% for cost efficiency while preserving headroom for bursts.
3. Identify upcoming model rollouts and consult the model-onboarding team for perf profiles and quantization recommendations.
4. Authorize purchase/lease of additional capacity if projected utilization > 75% in 60 days.
5. Test autoscaling policies in staging with synthetic traffic that emulates production p95 patterns.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Investment Prioritization

Quarterly reliability process
- Each quarter teams propose reliability initiatives tied to measurable KPIs (reduce p99 latency by X ms, lower mean time to recovery (MTTR) by Y minutes, reduce error budget burn by Z%).
- Initiative selection criteria: customer impact (severity x frequency), cost/effort estimate, cross-team dependencies, and effect on error budget or SLOs.
- Funded initiatives become tracked epics with an SRE sponsor and product owner.

Example initiatives
- Adaptive batching and KV-prefetching for recurrent inference workloads to cut per-token latency by 15%.
- Circuit breaker and backpressure mechanism for downstream storage and third-party APIs.
- Improved model fallback paths: lightweight quantized variant automatically served when heavy models exceed latency SLOs.

4) Incident Review Standards and Postmortems

Incident triage and response
- Severity definitions: Sev1 (service unavailable/high customer impact), Sev2 (degraded functionality), Sev3 (minor impact/partial degradation).
- Incident commander (IC) roles: lead, communications, tech lead, SRE liaison. Clearly document IC rotation and escalation contact list in the on-call schedule.

Postmortem requirements (for Sev1/Sev2 incidents)
- Complete postmortem published within 72 hours of incident resolution. Postmortem must include: timeline, impact statement (customers affected, error budget consumed), root cause analysis (RCA) with evidence, detection and response timeline, action items with owners and due dates, and verification plan.
- All Sev1 action items must have owners and due dates and are tracked in the reliability OKR board. Action items must be verified in a follow-up review within 30 days.

Learning and blameless culture
- Postmortems must be blameless and focus on systemic fixes. Use the "why/why" method to avoid single-person blame and identify process, tooling, or design gaps.

5) Operational Tooling

Required tooling surface
- Metrics: central Prometheus/ClickHouse metrics with standard SRE dashboards (SLOs, error budget burn, capacity utilization).
- Tracing: distributed traces captured (Tempo-compatible) with standardized span tags (service, operation, model_id, request_type).
- Logging: structured logs (JSON) forwarded to central logging (ELK/Clickhouse) with 30-day hot retention and 180-day cold retention for security/compliance-critical services.
- Alerting: routed via PagerDuty with deduplicated alert rules; alerts must map to runbooks.
- Chaos and load-testing: ChaosMonkey-style fault injection in staging, and k6-based load tests for automated scaling validation.

Alerting standards
- Alert triage rules: actionable, owner-assigned, and runbook-linked. Avoid alerts that fire during routine maintenance.
- Alert severity mapping must align with incident sev definitions and include escalation paths (on-call -> second on-call -> tech lead -> engineering manager).

Operational dashboards (minimum set)
- SLO overview: current attainment and 30-day window.
- Error budget burn: burn rate heatmap by service and recent deploys.
- Capacity dashboard: GPU pool utilization, instance age/health, pending growth requests.
- Latency profiles: p50/p95/p99 by endpoint and model, with heatmap for token-length buckets.

6) SRE Runbooks (canonical template)

Runbook principles
- Runbooks must be concise, tested, and include the minimal set of commands/actions to restore service or mitigate customer impact.
- Each runbook must list preconditions, detection signals, impact assessment steps, mitigation steps, rollback criteria, and post-incident verification.

Canonical runbook template
- title: short descriptive name
- service: owning service name
- severity: sev1|sev2|sev3
- detection: metric/alert name and threshold
- impact: who and how many customers are affected
- immediate_actions: numbered steps for on-call to follow (with exact CLI commands or dashboard links)
- escalation: contacts and escalation timeouts
- rollback_criteria: clear conditions to roll back a deployment or change
- verification: how to confirm service healthy after mitigation
- owner: runbook owner and last test date

Example runbook: High 95th Percentile Latency on redwood-api-generation
- title: high-p95-latency-redwood-api-generation
- service: redwood-api-generation
- severity: sev2
- detection: alerts/http_p95_latency{service="redwood-api-generation"} > 350ms for 5m
- impact: increased latency for text generation requests; ~12% of requests exceed target causing client timeouts.
- immediate_actions:
  1. Check recent deploys: curl -s https://ci.internal/api/latest-deploys?service=redwood-api-generation
  2. Verify queue/backpressure: kubectl -n inference get hpa,deploy | grep redwood-api-generation
  3. Toggle adaptive batching to conservative mode: POST to https://ops-api.internal/v1/configs/redwood-api-generation with body '{"batching_profile":"conservative"}'
  4. If latency remains high after 10 minutes, scale GPU pool by +20% from the autoscaling dashboard and notify SRE lead.
  5. If scaling and batching don't help, roll back last deploy: ci rollback --service redwood-api-generation --to-tag <last-good-tag>
- escalation: if unresolved in 30 minutes, page on-call escalation and open Sev2 incident channel (#inc-sev2-redwood-api).
- rollback_criteria: clear p95 improvement to < 300ms after rollback for 10 minutes and error budget burn normalizes.
- verification: monitor SLO dashboard and run synthetic requests (1000 requests at 95th token length).
- owner: redwood-api-generation-sre (last_tested: 2027-02-10)

Runbook testing and exercises
- Runbooks must be tested annually (tabletop) and after significant platform changes. Testing results and gaps must be recorded in the runbook metadata.

7) Ownership, On-call, and Escalation

On-call rotations
- SRE rotations published in the on-call schedule with primary/secondary roles. Primary handles first response; secondary supports escalation and tooling.
- Ensure replacement coverage for planned time off.

Escalation policy
- Escalation timeouts are 5 minutes (primary), 10 minutes (secondary), 20 minutes (tech lead), 30 minutes (engineering manager) for Sev1 incidents.

8) Metrics and Reporting

Quarterly reporting
- Each service reports SLO attainment, error budget consumption, incident counts by severity, MTTR, and progress on reliability initiatives as part of the SRE Quarterly Report.

KPIs tracked weekly
- SLO attainment (30-day), error budget burn-rate (1d, 7d), active incidents, average MTTR, and capacity headroom per critical pool.

Appendices and References

- See eng-infra/capacity-planning templates for spreadsheet and forecasting artifacts.
